questions.q: Why does PowerShell use -lt and -eq instead of < and ==?
options: The punctuation symbols < and > are already reserved for redirecting output to a file
PowerShell doesn't support comparison operators at all
-lt and -eq only work inside a switch statement
It's a legacy typo that Microsoft never fixed
questions.explain: < and > are redirection operators, a holdover from the shell's command-line roots, so comparisons use letter-based operators instead.

questions.q: What does the default block in a switch statement do?
options: It runs when none of the other cases match — the switch equivalent of a final else
It always runs first, before any other case is checked
It deletes the variable being switched on
It is required syntax with no functional effect
questions.explain: default is the fallback case, exactly like else at the end of an if/elseif chain.

questions.q: When is switch genuinely preferable to a chain of elseifs, according to this lesson?
options: When you're matching one variable against a list of known, discrete values — it avoids repeating the variable comparison on every line
switch is always strictly faster to execute than if/elseif in every case
switch should be used instead of if/elseif in literally every situation, with no exceptions
switch cannot be used with string values, only numbers
questions.explain: The lesson frames it as a readability choice for discrete-value matching, not a universal replacement or a performance claim.

questions.q: In the example, what determines whether if or elseif is a better fit than switch?
options: Whether the branches are based on a genuine condition or range (use if/elseif) versus matching discrete known values (use switch)
if/elseif can only be used with numbers, never strings
switch cannot have more than two cases
There is no meaningful difference and the choice is arbitrary
questions.explain: Range/condition-based logic (like disk space thresholds) fits if/elseif; discrete value matching (like a status field) fits switch.

questions.q: In the disk-space example, what triggers the WARNING branch?
options: Free space that is less than 20 GB but not less than 5 GB
Free space that is exactly 0 GB
Free space greater than 100 GB
The WARNING branch never actually runs in that example
questions.explain: The elseif checks -lt 20 only after the first -lt 5 check already failed, so it catches the 5-20 GB range.
